title: What flood insurance training do agents need to sell NFIP policies?
description: NFIP flood insurance agent training: section 207 of the Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2004, FEMA's 2005 course outline, and verified New York and Texas rules.
shortAnswer: Section 207 of the Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2004 directed the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to set minimum training and education requirements for all insurance agents who sell National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) policies. FEMA's 2005 notice chose to implement them through state licensing and continuing education, built around a basic flood course outline and a model 3 hour course. States set the hours: New York requires 3 hours of enhanced flood instruction for agents selling NFIP policies.
keyTakeaways: Section 207 of the Bunning-Bereuter-Blumenauer Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2004 (Pub. L. 108-264, signed June 30, 2004) required FEMA to establish minimum training requirements for all agents selling flood insurance and publish them in the Federal Register within 6 months.

FEMA's notice of September 1, 2005 (70 FR 52117) chose to work through state insurance departments rather than set a separate federal license, citing Senate report language against duplicative requirements.

The notice pointed states to the NCOIL model act, which calls for flood knowledge at prelicensing and a one-time 3 hour flood CE course for existing producers, and set out a basic flood insurance course outline.

New York requires at least 1 hour of flood instruction per licensing period for property and casualty licensees and at least 3 hours of enhanced flood instruction for those selling NFIP policies, for licenses renewing on or after April 1, 2022.
Texas certifies a flood course of at least 3 hours under 28 TAC section 19.1021, built on FEMA's outline, which may be taken up to 12 months before licensing and counted toward initial CE.
jurisdiction: United States (federal NFIP requirement implemented through state insurance regulation; New York and Texas as verified examples)
regulator: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), which administers the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), working through state insurance departments including the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) and the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI)
appliesTo: Licensed property and casualty insurance agents who sell Standard Flood Insurance Policies through the NFIP
Agents of insurers in the NFIP Write Your Own (WYO) Program
Property and casualty licensees in states, such as New York, that require flood content for all such licensees
Continuing education providers offering state-approved flood courses

sections.heading: What does section 207 of the Flood Insurance Reform Act require?

blocks.text: Section 207 required FEMA to set minimum training and education requirements for agents who sell flood insurance, working with the industry and state regulators. It is codified as a note to [42 U.S.C. 4011](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/4011), as at November 2026.

blocks.title: Flood Insurance Reform Act of 2004, section 207
blocks.text: "The Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency shall, in cooperation with the insurance industry, State insurance regulators, and other interested parties (1) establish minimum training and education requirements for all insurance agents who sell flood insurance policies; and (2) not later than 6 months after the date of enactment of this Act, publish these requirements in the Federal Register, and inform insurance companies and agents of the requirements."
The Act was signed on June 30, 2004. Section 207 does not set hours or a course, and it does not create a federal flood agent license. It placed the design decision with FEMA, which made it in 2005.

sections.heading: How did FEMA implement the training requirement?

blocks.text: FEMA implemented section 207 through existing state licensing and CE systems rather than a separate federal requirement. Its notice, [Flood Insurance Training and Education Requirements for Insurance Agents](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/fr/70/52117?link-type=html), was published in the Federal Register on September 1, 2005 (70 FR 52117 to 52119, RIN 1660-ZA06).

The notice explains the choice. It quotes Senate Report 108-262, which asked FEMA to avoid burdening agents with inconsistent state and federal requirements and to work through the states' existing CE processes. It also notes that the McCarran-Ferguson Act excludes federal insurance programs, including the NFIP, from state regulation, so FEMA could lawfully set its own standards but chose not to duplicate state schemes.

FEMA committed to give states expertise on course content, access to NFIP training modules, and updates when NFIP policy or procedures change. For states without a flood training program, it pointed to the State Flood Disaster Mitigation and Relief Model Act adopted by the National Conference of Insurance Legislators (NCOIL) on November 21, 2003. That model requires resident producer applicants to show satisfactory knowledge of flood insurance and the NFIP to be licensed, and requires producers already licensed to complete a one-time 3 hour flood CE course, earning 3 hours of CE credit.

The 2005 notice also described incentives then in place, including an additional 25 percent in NFIP Agent Co-op advertising funds for agents who had completed a state-approved flood CE course within the past 12 months. Current incentive programs should be confirmed with FEMA, as the notice reflects 2005 arrangements.

sections.heading: What does the basic flood insurance course cover?

blocks.text: FEMA's notice set a basic flood insurance course outline in eight sections, intended to give agents a basic understanding of the NFIP they can share with customers. Texas reproduces the outline in [28 TAC section 19.1021(g)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/texas/28-Tex-Admin-Code-SS-19-1021).

items: **Introduction:** NFIP background, community participation, the Emergency and Regular Programs, the Community Rating System, eligible buildings, the Coastal Barrier Resources System, and who needs flood insurance, including mandatory purchase in high-risk zones.
**Flood maps and zone determinations:** Flood Hazard Boundary Maps, Flood Insurance Rate Maps, pre-FIRM and post-FIRM buildings, Special Flood Hazard Areas and base flood elevation.

**Policies and products:** the Dwelling, General Property and Residential Condominium Building Association policies, key definitions, and property covered and not covered, including basements and Increased Cost of Compliance coverage.
**General rules:** statutory coverage limits, deductibles, loss settlement on actual cash value or replacement cost, no binders, one building per policy, and the waiting period.
**Rating:** elevated buildings, buildings with basements, when to use an Elevation Certificate, and grandfathering.
**Claims handling:** helping the client file a claim, the appeals process and the claims handbook.
**Requirements of the 2004 Act:** point of sale and renewal duties, including explaining coverages purchased, exclusions, how losses are adjusted, and acknowledgement forms.
**Agent resources:** Write Your Own companies, FEMA websites and the Flood Insurance Manual.

blocks.text: The notice adds that agents should take further training regularly to understand more advanced flood topics. That expectation fits an annual or per-renewal cycle; the guide on [setting mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) explains how to set one.

New York builds flood content into its 15 credit producer CE requirement. The [NYDFS continuing education page](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/apps_and_licensing/agents_and_brokers/continuing_education) states that, effective November 12, 2021, the 15 credits under Insurance Law section 2132 must include at least one hour of flood insurance instruction for licensees selling one or more property and casualty lines, and at least three hours of enhanced flood insurance instruction for licensees who sell flood insurance through the NFIP.

These requirements apply to licenses renewing on or after April 1, 2022, and CE must be completed before the renewal or relicensing application is submitted. NYDFS also publishes a flood insurance training and providers listing. New York's other topic minimums, such as ethics and bias, are covered on the page on [insurance producer continuing education requirements](/regulations/insurance-producer-continuing-education-requirements).

Texas certifies a flood insurance course that implements FEMA's standards. 28 TAC section 19.1021(a) states that it establishes FEMA's September 1, 2005 standards for a department-certified CE course, and section 19.1021(b) requires the course to be at least three hours long and to cover the outline topics.

items: **Timing:** the course may be taken after licensing or within 12 months before the license issue date (19.1021(d)).
**Credit:** up to three hours count toward the initial CE requirement when the course is completed before licensing (19.1021(e)).
**Records:** proof of pre-licensing completion must be kept for four years or through the second license renewal, whichever is longer, and produced to TDI on request (19.1021(e)).
**Proof:** a provider-issued completion certificate meeting section 19.1011(e) demonstrates completion (19.1021(f)).

blocks.text: Section 19.1003(a)(2)(A) carves this course out of the general rule that CE taken before licensing does not count, as described on the page on [Texas insurance adjuster continuing education](/regulations/texas-insurance-adjuster-continuing-education).

blocks.text: Because the federal requirement is delivered through state rules, an agency writing NFIP business in several states must map each producer to each state's flood rule. The table shows the obligations verified on this page.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats FEMA's eight section outline as the base knowledge framework and attaches each state's hour and timing rule to it as a separate obligation. When FEMA changes NFIP procedures, the affected outline topics, and the producers who need updated training, are identified from the framework.

faqs.q: Is there a federal flood insurance license for agents?
faqs.a: No. Section 207 asked FEMA to set minimum training requirements, and FEMA's 2005 notice chose to implement them through state licensing and continuing education rather than a separate federal credential. Agents need a state property and casualty license and must meet their state's flood training rules.

faqs.q: How many hours of flood training are required?
faqs.a: It depends on the state. The NCOIL model that FEMA pointed to uses a one-time 3 hour course. New York requires 3 hours of enhanced flood instruction each licensing period for NFIP sellers, and 1 hour for other property and casualty licensees. Texas certifies a course of at least 3 hours.

faqs.q: Do flood training hours count toward general CE?
faqs.a: Generally yes. The NCOIL model awards 3 hours of CE credit for its flood course, New York counts flood instruction within the 15 required credits, and Texas lets up to 3 pre-licensing flood hours count toward the initial CE requirement.

faqs.q: Does the requirement apply to adjusters?
faqs.a: Section 207 refers to insurance agents who sell flood insurance policies, so it is a sales requirement and does not set adjuster training. Adjuster licensing and continuing education are set separately by each state; see the pages on Texas and Florida insurance adjuster continuing education.

FEMA notice, 70 FR 52117-52119, September 1, 2005, RIN 1660-ZA06: Pub. L. 108-264 signed June 30, 2004; quotes S. Rep. No. 108-262 on avoiding inconsistent state and federal requirements; McCarran-Ferguson excludes the NFIP from state regulation; FEMA chose to implement through state licensing and CE.

FEMA 2005 notice: NCOIL State Flood Disaster Mitigation and Relief Model Act adopted November 21, 2003 requires prelicensing flood knowledge and a one-time 3 hour flood CE course earning 3 hours credit; additional 25 percent Agent Co-op funds for agents completing a state-approved flood CE course within the past 12 months; basic flood insurance course outline; agents should take additional training on a regular basis.

NYDFS: 15 CE credits under Insurance Law 2132; effective November 12, 2021 at least one hour flood instruction for property/casualty licensees and at least three hours enhanced flood instruction for NFIP sellers; applies to licenses renewing on or after April 1, 2022.
